sentences.text: The learned APP Ms.Deshmukh has however placed reliance upon the decision of Constitution Bench of the Apex Court in case of Laxman Vs. State of Maharashtra, 3 in support of her submission that absence of Doctor's certification as to mental fitness of the declarant, is not a sine qua non, and she would submit that the endorsement indicating that the patient was 1 2022(4) BCR (Cri) 781 2 2021 6 SCC 213 3 (2002) 6 SCC 710 Tilak 11/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc conscious, is sufficient to prove that deceased was in a fit mental condition to make the Dying Declaration.

In addition, she would submit that when the expert witness like the Medical Officer has deposed before the Court that the deceased was in a fit and conscious state to make the declaration, the medical opinion shall prevail, and in absence of certification of the Doctor, as to the fitness of mind of the declarant, the Dying Declaration will not become inadmissible if it otherwise inspire confidence.
Ms. Deshmukh would submit that there is no requirement of law that a Dying Declaration must necessarily be made to a Magistrate, and when such statement is recorded by Magistrate, there is no specific statutory form in which it should be recorded.

In addition, she would also place reliance upon another decision of the Apex Court in case of State of Jharkhand vs. Shailendra Kumar Rai,4 holding that Dying Declaration ought to be ideally recorded by the Magistrate if possible, but if it is recorded by police personnel, it cannot be said to be completely inadmissible for that reason alone,
and also if the Dying Declaration recorded is not in form of Question and Answers, it will not affect it's admissibility or probative value.

sentences.text: The Dying Declaration at Exhibit-22 is recorded by PW 2, who was attached to Haveli police station and posted in Sassoon Chowky.

On receiving information, he visited Ward 4 AIR 2022 SC 5393 Tilak 12/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc No.25 where Mangal was admitted, and he indicated to the Medical Officer, on duty, that he wanted to record the statement of the patient and ascertain from him whether she was in a position to give the statement.
The Medical Officer accompanied him and confirmed that the patient was in a fully conscious condition and permitted recording of the statement.

The version of PW 2 is corroborated by PW 6, as he confirmed that he made endorsement on the statement regarding the state of patient and on being confronted with Exhibit-22, identified the endorsement and his signature.
PW 6 categorically deposed that at the time, the statement was being recorded, the patient was conscious and she was in a state of making valid statement.

In the cross- examination, he also admit that when the statement was recorded at about 2.00 p.m, at that time, he alone was present with the police personnel, who was recording the statement and categorically denied the suggestion that her mother was also present when the statement was being recorded.

15 As regards the second Dying Declaration that is recorded by PW 4 (Exhibit 34), which is recorded on directions of Sr.P.I of Shirur police station, PW 4 has also deposed that he made inquiry with the Doctor, whether the lady admitted in Ward No.25 of Sassoon Hospital was in the condition of giving the statement and he was accompanied by the doctor, when he Tilak 13/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc Gahininath Ramchandra Sankpal vs The State Of Maharashtra on 10 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198287414/

sentences.text: PW 6 has corroborated PW 4, by stating that the statement of the patient was recorded at about 5.30 p.m, and he was present during recording of the statement and the patient was to be conscious and in a state of making valid statement and accordingly, put his endorsement on Exhibit-34.
He also deposed that the patient was under his treatment till he succumbed to the injuries.

16 The reading of the evidence of PW 2 and PW 4 along with Exhibits 22 and 34, the role of the accused in the entire incident, has clearly surfaced on record, as the deceased categorically gave a statement that she poured kerosene on her person, but it is the accused who set her on fire.

17 The argument of Mr.Shivarkar that the statement of the deceased is not recorded by the Executive Magistrate, in any way, do not affect the veracity of Exhibit-22 and 34 recorded by the police personnel.
The law, as regards the recording of Dying Declaration and its admissibility and reliability, is by now well settled.
A Dying Declaration can be the sole basis of conviction even without corroboration if it inspire confidence.

The only requirement, which the Court must ensure is that the person making such a declaration was in a fit state of mind at the time of Tilak 14/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc making the statement and the statement was voluntary and was not an outcome of some act of tutoring,
prompting or imagination.

When the Dying Declaration is suspicious or suffer from any infirmity,
the Court may require some corroborative evidence before relying upon the same.

Similarly, there is no requirement of recording a Dying Declaration by a particular person in position or it being recorded in prescribed format or by following prescribed procedure, but it is important for the person who is recording the Dying Declaration to be satisfied that the maker is in a fit state of mind and capable of making statement, though recording of a Dying Declaration by a Magistrate does ensure its authenticity and credibility, but a Dying Declaration recorded by a police personnel do not lose its credibility, merely because it is not recorded by the Magistrate, if the declaration is otherwise true and voluntary.

The evidentiary value to be attached to a statement which is made by a person, which amounts to a Dying Declaration necessarily depends on facts and circumstances of each individual case, and once it is established by the prosecution that while the person gave the statement, he or she was in a fit state of mind to make the statement, and that the statement was voluntary, a conviction based on such statement would not warrant any interference.

In case of multiple Dying Declarations, unless and until the declarations suffer from inconsistency,
of such a nature, that the maker of the statement could not be believed at all, the Court would safely rely upon such declarations and ignore minor inconsistency/discrepancy.

18 In case of Lakhan Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, 5 the law with regard to Dying Declaration was summarized by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the following words:-
"21

entities.text: Lakhan Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In view of the above, the law on the issue of dying declaration can be summarized to the effect that in case, the Court comes to the conclusion that the dying declaration is true and reliable, has been recorded by a person at a time when the deceased was fit physically and mentally to make the declaration and it has not been made under any tutoring/duress/prompting; it can be the sole basis for recording conviction.
In such an eventuality no corroboration is required.

In case, there are multiple dying declarations and there are inconsistencies between them, generally, the dying declaration recorded by the higher officer like a Magistrate can be relied upon,
provided that there is no circumstance giving rise to any suspicion about its truthfulness.

In case, there are circumstances wherein the declaration had been made, not voluntarily and even otherwise, it is not supported by the other evidence,
the Court has to scrutinize the facts of an individual case very carefully and take a decision as to which of the declarations is worth reliance."

19 In light of the above position of law, when we have examined the two Dying Declarations, it definitely meet the test of law, as the deceased had specifically assigned the role of setting her ablaze to the appellant and on this material aspect, we do not find any inconsistency.

As regards the subsequent act about who 5 (2010) 8 SCC 514 Tilak 16/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc took her to the hospital, there is some inconsistency, as in her second declaration at Exhibit-34, she stated that when she screamed, her brother-in-law Sampat extinguished the fire and took her to Sassoon Hospital, whereas in the first statement (Exhibit-22), she stated that the persons in the neighborhood extinguished the fire.
However, she has remained consistent about her accusation against her husband of setting her on fire.
The Doctor has certified on both the statements of the deceased recorded by PW 2 and 4, that she was in fit state of mind to give the statement.
We therefore find the Dying Declaration to be truthful and reliable, as immediately after Mangal was brought to the hospital, both the Dying Declarations were recorded.

Both the statements given by the deceased inspire confidence and since PW 6, the Doctor, was also cross-examined extensively,
but he has confirmed that the patient was in fit state of mind when her statement was being recorded, he remained present at the bed- side of the maker of the statement, there is no reason why we should doubt the veracity of the said statement and that too, merely on the ground that the statement is not recorded by a Magistrate.

sentences.text: Not giving of the separate certificate by Doctor also do not affect the credibility of the statement since the doctor has endorsed that the patient was in a fit state of mind and capable of making the statement, and in the witness box, he admitted that he Tilak 17/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc had made endorsement to that effect of both the Dying Declarations.

Since the juristic theory regarding acceptability of a Dying Declaration is that it is a statement made by a person, who is at the door step of death and when every hope of this world has failed, such a person, and at this stage, when every motive to falsehood is silenced, and in this scenario, the man is induced by the most powerful consideration to speak only the truth, though it is necessary before such a statement is accepted as gospel truth, to ensure that the declaration is made to a person who can be relied upon and also upon being declared to be in a fit state of mind to make such a statement.

Essentially, what is required before recording of such a statement is mental fitness of a person to give the statement, and therefore, when a statement made by a maker is found to be voluntary and truthful, it can form the basis of conviction of an accused.

21 Once we have accepted the statement of deceased Mangal to be voluntary and truthful, and not being a tutored one, if we look at the accusation faced by the appellant, her husband, it is voluntarily seen that on the date of incident, i.e. 24/9/90, when she was present in the house, being unwell, and asked her husband to be taken for treatment, he got irritated.

When he refused to take her to the hospital and uttered that she shall die, Tilak 18/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc she also felt frustrated and as per her own version, in fit of anger, she poured kerosene on her person.
Her husband also in fit of anger lighted the match-stick and set her on fire.

The aforesaid version of the deceased Mangal reflect that the quibble occurred on her insistence to take her to a doctor, and it is she who poured kerosene on her person in a fit of rage, and this irked the appellant and he, at the spur of the moment, set her ablaze.

From the arrest panchnama, it is also seen that the appellant had sustained boils on her palm,
indicative of his attempt to extinguish the fire.

His presence on the spot is further established, as the clothes which were produced at the time of arrest, which he was wearing at the time of incident,
smelled of kerosene and traces of kerosene were revealed during it's analysis.
22

On appreciation of evidence, we can notice that though the appellant had the knowledge that his act of igniting the match-stick and throwing it at his wife Mangal, is likely to set her ablaze and may result in her death, but from the narration of the deceased in form of two Dying Declarations, it is evident that he had no intention to commit her murder.
Punishment for culpable homicide, not amounting to murder, where the act is committed without intention, but with knowledge, is specifically prescribed under Part-II of Section 304 of IPC.

24 In Vithal Sadashiv Gaikwad Vs. The State of Maharashtra,6 this Court by referring to the decision of Supreme Court in Paniben Vs. State of Gujarat,7 where the law with regard to Dying Declaration was discussed, pronounced upon a scenario of unhappy marriage, and the chance of falsely implicating a spouse or a relative and this is specifically expressed in the following words :-

entities.text: Vithal Sadashiv Gaikwad Vs. The State of Maharashtra,6
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "15 In Paniben's, case the Supreme Court had occasion to consider the law with regard to dying declarations threadbare.
The Supreme Court however did not have occasion to consider one more aspect that needs to be taken very serious note of particularly in cases of the present type.

Where there is a background of unhappiness,
marital discord, violence, accusations against fidelity and the like and where it is highly suggestive of the fact that the deceased wife has been the victim of harassment torture, and character assasination over a period of time and consequently can never be favourably disposed towards the husband, the Court would have to put itself on guard.

In such cases the principle "Nemo moriturus proesumitur ementiri" the principle which governs the credibility that is attributed to dying declarations,
namely that a dying person would not normally tell a lie, does require serious examination

Having regard to the mental disposition of the victim one cannot tute out the possibility on the part of some persons to implicate, purely out of a sense of vendetta, the husband who has been responsible for prolonged and protracted ill-treatment.

Cases are quite common where the wife is virtually pushed to a position of a utter desperation and which results in an attempted suicide and at a later point of time when questions are put one cannot completely eliminate the possibility of false implication, if the background has 6 (1994) 1 Bom.C.R 702 7 (1992) 2 SCC 474 Tilak 20/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc been extremely hostile, and the victim feels guilty having attempted the suicide.
That aspect therefore does require serious examination.

The law, as regards the recording of Dying Declaration and its admissibility and reliability, is by now well settled.
A Dying Declaration can be the sole basis of conviction even without corroboration if it inspire confidence.
The only requirement, which the Court must ensure is that the person making such a declaration was in a fit state of mind at the time of Tilak 14/21 APEAL 1269-13 J.doc making the statement and the statement was voluntary and was not an outcome of some act of tutoring,
prompting or imagination.
When the Dying Declaration is suspicious or suffer from any infirmity,
the Court may require some corroborative evidence before relying upon the same.
Similarly, there is no requirement of recording a Dying Declaration by a particular person in position or it being recorded in prescribed format or by following prescribed procedure, but it is important for the person who is recording the Dying Declaration to be satisfied that the maker is in a fit state of mind and capable of making statement, though recording of a Dying Declaration by a Magistrate does ensure its authenticity and credibility, but a Dying Declaration recorded by a police personnel do not lose its credibility, merely because it is not recorded by the Magistrate, if the declaration is otherwise true and voluntary.
The evidentiary value to be attached to a statement which is made by a person, which amounts to a Dying Declaration necessarily depends on facts and circumstances of each individual case, and once it is established by the prosecution that while the person gave the statement, he or she was in a fit state of mind to make the statement, and that the statement was voluntary, a conviction based on such statement would not warrant any interference.

of such a nature, that the maker of the statement could not be believed at all, the Court would safely rely upon such declarations and ignore minor inconsistency/discrepancy.
Both the statements given by the deceased inspire confidence and since PW 6, the Doctor, was also cross-examined extensively,
but he has confirmed that the patient was in fit state of mind when her statement was being recorded, he remained present at the bed- side of the maker of the statement, there is no reason why we should doubt the veracity of the said statement and that too, merely on the ground that the statement is not recorded by a Magistrate.
Since the juristic theory regarding acceptability of a Dying Declaration is that it is a statement made by a person, who is at the door step of death and when every hope of this world has failed, such a person, and at this stage, when every motive to falsehood is silenced, and in this scenario, the man is induced by the most powerful consideration to speak only the truth, though it is necessary before such a statement is accepted as gospel truth, to ensure that the declaration is made to a person who can be relied upon and also upon being declared to be in a fit state of mind to make such a statement.
Essentially, what is required before recording of such a statement is mental fitness of a person to give the statement, and therefore, when a statement made by a maker is found to be voluntary and truthful, it can form the basis of conviction of an accused.

Punishment for culpable homicide, not amounting to murder, where the act is committed without intention, but with knowledge, is specifically prescribed under Part-II of Section 304 of IPC.
